sections.html:
Quincy anchors Adams County, the westernmost county in Illinois, which touches Missouri along its western edge. A property sale touches four offices: the collector, the Supervisor of Assessments, a township assessor and the Board of Review.

The collector, who is also the county treasurer, sends bills and takes payments at 507 Vermont St, Suite G12, Quincy (217-277-2245). The Supervisor of Assessments runs exemptions and equalization. The Board of Review hears assessment complaints in the Adams County Courthouse. The county has 23 townships, so a house outside Quincy is usually valued by a township assessor and not by a city office.

About the local market: population is 64,267 for 2025, down from 65,737 in 2020. Owners live in 72.1% of households, the middle owned home is worth $162,600, and renters typically pay $828.

sections.h2: How the tax cycle works for a seller
sections.html:
Bills trail the assessment by a year. An assessment reflects the home's value and exemptions on January 1, and the tax on it is paid the following year. A seller who closes mid-year therefore still owes for a stretch the county has not yet billed.

After a deed is recorded, the owner of record answers for later bills. Mailing happens in late spring. The first installment falls around June 1, or 30 days after mailing if that is later, and the second around September 1. A buyer may pay both halves at once or in two equal payments.

Typical Adams County collection calendar
StepUsual timing
Real estate bills mailedLate spring
First installment dueAround June 1, or 30 days after mailing if later
Second installment dueAround September 1
$10 mail and publication fee addedAround October 1
Last day to pay before the saleLate October
Annual tax saleLate October

Several dates are tentative each year, so ask the collector for the calendar covering the tax year you are closing in.

sections.h2: Late payments and the tax sale
sections.html:
For tax paid after September 30, the collector accepts a cashier's check, money order, cash or a card. Personal, business and e-checks are turned away. State law sets late interest at 1 1/2% per month or fraction of a month, and mail postmarked by the due date counts as on time (35 ILCS 200/21-15).

After the October fee the county publishes its list of delinquent parcels, and one last day remains for card payments ahead of the sale. Clear any unpaid tax before then, since a parcel sold at tax sale clouds the title.

  • Ask the collector at 217-277-2245 whether an installment is open before you list.
  • A title agent's tax search puts any payoff on the settlement statement.
  • Hold on to the postmarked envelope or bank confirmation when you pay near a deadline.

A home outside Cook County is assessed at 33 1/3 percent of market value. To check your own number, divide the assessed value by what you think the home would sell for, then compare that ratio with similar homes nearby.

Put your complaint to the Board of Review in writing. In a county with fewer than 150,000 residents the filing date is August 10, though a missed publishing date can push it back. Sessions are usually Monday through Thursday, 8:30 to 11:30 a.m., from July 10 to October 7. The Board reads your complaint and mails a tentative decision. After that you can request a hearing, with or without an attorney.

A tax bill is outside the Board's reach. What it adjusts is the assessment behind the bill, and once it adjourns it prints the list of changes in a county newspaper. Still unhappy? Appeal in writing to the State Property Tax Appeal Board.

  • Strong grounds: a value estimate above what the home would sell for, wrong lot or building measurements, or an assessment above those of similar neighbors.
  • Helpful evidence: your deed or transfer declaration, a current appraisal, nearby comparable sales with photos, and the property record card.
  • A complaint filed late cannot fix a bill that has already gone out.

Each amount below comes off equalized assessed value and not the bill itself. The Supervisor of Assessments can tell you which ones fit your situation.

  • General homestead: the growth in equalized value since 1977, to a ceiling of $6,000, where the owner lives in the house.
  • Senior citizens: $5,000 off equalized value, available at 65.
  • Senior assessment freeze: household income capped at $75,000, renewed each year.
  • Homestead improvement: value from new construction, at most $75,000 a year, running four years after the work is finished and occupied.
  • Returning service members: $5,000 for two consecutive years.
  • Disabled persons: $2,000, applied for every year.
  • Disabled service members, standard exemption: $2,500 for a rating from 30% up to 50%, $5,000 from 50% up to 70%, and total relief from 70%.

Nearly all require you to live in the house. A buyer therefore files a fresh application once they hold title.

Owners who qualify may put off as much as $7,500 of tax a year under the state's Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Program. The deferral accrues simple interest at 3 percent from tax year 2023 on, and the county places a lien on the house. To apply you must be 65 by June 1, earn $65,000 or less as a household, and have lived three years in the home or a similar qualifying one.

A sale or transfer cannot legally close and record until the deferred amounts are paid, and the balance comes due 90 days after a sale. Filing is in person at the treasurer's office from January 1 through March 1. If you hold a deferral, get a payoff figure from the treasurer early and have it settled from your proceeds.

The collector's office is inside the North 5th Street entrance of the courthouse, staffed on weekdays from half past eight until half past four.

  • Online by e-check or card: $1.50 per e-check and 2.25% of the payment for cards ($2.00 minimum).
  • A drop box outside the North 5th Street entrance, open around the clock (no cash).
  • Mail to Adams County Collector, 507 Vermont St STE G12, Quincy, IL 62301-2998, where the postmark date counts.
  • Participating banks, for real estate tax only and never after the due date.
  • Bank bill pay, using the full parcel number without dashes as the account.

Tax records and duplicate bills are online at no charge through the county's tax lookup.

The closing statement may include a credit from the seller for estimated unbilled and unpaid tax. The exact figure is unknown until bills are created. In most cases the new owner receives the next bill and pays the seller's share. Give the buyer or title company a mailing address, since the county uses one address for bills, assessment notices and legal notices.

The office pauses deed and address updates for one to two weeks in mid-April while bills are produced. Splits and combined parcels recorded after August 10 do not take effect until January of the next tax year, and the original owner still gets the original bill. Decide in the contract who pays it.

faqs.q: When are Adams County property tax installments due?
faqs.a: Around June 1 (or 30 days after mailing if later) and around September 1. The date printed on your bill is the one that counts.

faqs.q: What if my Quincy-area tax bill never arrives?
faqs.a: Phone the collector at 217-277-2245. Tax records and duplicate bills are online at no charge.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Adams County assessment after August 10?
faqs.a: Not normally. For counties under 150,000 residents that is the Board of Review filing date, though it can be extended when publishing dates were missed. Ask the Supervisor of Assessments which date applies to your township.

faqs.q: Will the senior deferral stop me from selling a house in Adams County?
faqs.a: It will not stop a sale, but it must be paid first. No transfer may be closed and recorded until deferred taxes and interest are paid, so request a payoff early.

faqs.q: Does the Board of Review lower my tax bill directly?
faqs.a: No. It changes the assessment, and the bill is then built from the new value. The Board has no authority to change a tax bill itself.
